name: LAMBADA
description: LAMBADA (LAnguage Modeling Broadened to Account for Discourse Aspects) is a dataset to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is a collection of narrative passages sharing the characteristic that human subjects are able to guess their last word if they are exposed to the whole passage, but not if they only see the last sentence preceding the target word. The dataset consists of 10,022 passages, divided into 4,869 development and 5,153 test passages extracted from novels.
creator: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández
citeAs: Denis Paperno, Germán Kruszewski, Angeliki Lazaridou, Quan Ngoc Pham, Raffaella Bernardi, Sandro Pezzelle, Marco Baroni, Gemma Boleda, Raquel Fernández. 2016. The LAMBADA dataset: Word prediction requiring a broad discourse context. In Proceedings of the 54th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, pages 1525–1534, Berlin, Germany.
rai:dataCollection: LAMBADA consists of passages composed of a context (on average 4.6 sentences) and a target sentence. The context size is the minimum number of complete sentences before the target sentence such that they cumulatively contain at least 50 tokens. The task is to guess the last word of the target sentence (the target word). The data come from the Book Corpus containing unpublished novels. The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The data come from the Book Corpus (Zhu et al., 2015), which contains unpublished novels. The corpus, after duplicate removal and filtering out of potentially offensive material with a stop word list, contains 5,325 novels and 465 million words.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Passages were filtered to reduce time and cost of dataset collection by excluding passages that are relatively easy for standard language models. A combination of four language models was used: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model). Any passage whose target word had probability ≥0.00175 according to any of the language models was excluded.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The corpus was randomly divided into equally-sized training and development+testing partitions. Passages were filtered using four language models to exclude relatively easy cases. The remaining passages were evaluated by human subjects through CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if correct, (2) a second subject guessed based on the whole passage; if also correct, (3) more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10. If no subject was able to guess the target word from the sentence alone, the passage was added to LAMBADA. In the crowdsourcing pipeline, 84–86% items were discarded at step 1, an additional 6–7% at step 2 and another 3–5% at step 3. Only about one in 25 input examples passed all the selection steps.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human subjects evaluated passages through the CrowdFlower crowdsourcing service in three steps: (1) one human subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if the guess was right, (2) a second subject guessed the target word based on the whole passage; if that guess was also right, (3) more subjects tried to guess the target word based on the target sentence only, until the word was guessed or the number of unsuccessful guesses reached 10. Subjects in step 3 were allowed 3 guesses per sentence. The criteria for passage inclusion were very strict: two consecutive subjects had to exactly match the missing word, and no subject (out of ten) was able to provide it based on local context only, even when given 3 guesses.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The strict perfect-match approach was used where only items that can be unambiguously determined by human subjects were kept. An alternative approach of including passages where broad-context subjects provided other plausible or synonymous continuations was considered but deemed not financially or practically feasible for a dataset of this scale.
rai:annotationsPerItem: Step 1: 1 subject; Step 2: 1 subject (if step 1 successful); Step 3: up to 10 subjects attempting to guess from sentence context only (with 3 guesses each)
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Four language models were used for filtering: a pre-trained recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov et al., 2011) and three models trained on the Book Corpus (a standard 4-gram model, a RNN and a feed-forward model)
rai:dataBiases: More than 80% of LAMBADA passages include the target word in the context, while in the input data that was the case for less than 15% of the passages. Most target words in LAMBADA are proper nouns (48%), followed by common nouns (37%) and verbs (7.7%). Proper nouns are hugely over-represented in LAMBADA, while the other categories are under-represented, compared to the POS distribution in the input. The LAMBADA items contain (quoted) direct speech significantly more often than the input items overall (71% of LAMBADA items vs. 61% of items in the input sample).
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset was designed to challenge language models with harder-than-average examples where broad context understanding is crucial. The strict perfect-match approach means that only items that can be unambiguously determined by human subjects were kept. The constraint that the target word be the last word of the sentence, while not necessary for the research goal, makes the task more natural for human subjects. The fact that the data contains unpublished novels minimizes the potential usefulness of general world knowledge and external resources for the task. LAMBADA passages are self-contained and cannot be solved by exploiting knowledge in the remainder of the novels.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is meant to evaluate the capabilities of computational models for text understanding by means of a word prediction task. It is intended as a challenging test set to encourage the development of new models capable of genuine understanding of broad context in natural language text. The training data (203 million words from 2,662 novels) can be used to train language models. The development data (4,869 passages) can be used to fine-tune models to the specifics of the LAMBADA passages. The test data (5,153 passages) is for evaluation.
